items.q: Which statement best reflects the security mindset?
options: Security is only a concern for big companies and banks
Security means hiding how your system works so attackers can't figure it out
Security is a property of how the system is built, so you design for it from the start
Security is a feature you add at the end, right before launch

explain.right: Security is a property of the design, not a bolt-on; you hold the defender's and attacker's viewpoints from the start.
explain.wrong: Bolting it on late is costly and leaky, hiding how things work ('obscurity') isn't security, and small apps get attacked too (bots scan everything).

items.q: Your plan is: 'nobody knows the secret admin URL, so it's safe.' What's wrong with relying on this?
options: Nothing — a hidden URL is a strong defense
Hidden URLs are fine as long as the site uses HTTPS
It only fails if you tell someone the URL
It's 'security through obscurity'; assume the attacker can discover how your system works, so the defense must hold anyway

explain.right: Obscurity isn't security: assume the attacker can read your code and find hidden paths, so real access control must protect the page.
explain.wrong: Hidden URLs leak through logs, referrers, and scanning; HTTPS protects the pipe, not the fact that the page is unprotected.

items.q: In threat modeling, a 'trust boundary' is:
options: A line where data crosses between something you control and something you don't (e.g. browser → your server)
A list of users you trust
The maximum number of requests allowed per second

explain.right: Trust boundaries are where data crosses in or out of your control; attacks concentrate there, so that's where you validate and authorize.
explain.wrong: It isn't a user list, a physical firewall, or a rate limit — it's the conceptual line where trust changes.

items.q: A lightweight threat model is essentially which set of questions?
options: How many users do we expect and how fast must the site load?
Who are my competitors and what features do they have?
Which antivirus should I buy, and how much does it cost?
What are we building? What can go wrong? What will we do about it? Did we do a good job?

explain.right: Those four questions are a real, usable threat model — specific to your app, they focus effort on the risks that matter.
explain.wrong: Antivirus, competitors, and performance are real concerns but aren't what threat modeling asks.

items.q: Pick one feature of your app and write one 'what would an attacker try?' question about it, plus the asset it threatens.
rubric: Names a concrete feature (e.g. 'view my profile', a login, a search box)
States a plausible attacker attempt (see another user's data, send weird input, guess a password)
Identifies the asset at risk (private data, account access, availability)

explain.right: Strong answers pair a specific attacker attempt with the concrete asset it would harm — that's the defender+attacker view in action.
explain.wrong: A weak answer stays vague ('someone could hack it') without naming the attempt or the asset.
